questions.q:
Here is a list of numbers.
21   23   25   27   29   31   33
From the list, write down
(a) a prime number greater than 25, [1]
(b) a cube number. [1]
questions.tip: 21 = 3 × 7, 25 = 5², 27 = 3³ and 33 = 3 × 11 are not prime: check small factors before you write an answer.

questions.q:
Without using a calculator, find the value of
(a) 64^(1/3), [1]
(b) (2/3)^(−3). [1]
questions.tip: A negative index means 'turn the fraction upside down' first, then apply the power to the top and the bottom.

questions.q:
p = 2³ × 3 × 5² and q = 2² × 3³ × 7.
(a) Find the highest common factor (HCF) of p and q. [1]
(b) Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of p and q. Give your answer as an ordinary number. [1]
(c) Find the smallest positive integer k such that pk is a square number. [2]
ms: (c) M1: recognises every prime must have an even power, e.g. 2⁴ × 3² × 5² or 'needs one more 2 and one more 3'
questions.model:
(a) Lowest power of each common prime: 2² × 3 = 12.
(b) Highest power of every prime: 2³ × 3³ × 5² × 7 = 8 × 27 × 25 × 7 = 37 800.
(c) p = 2³ × 3¹ × 5². For a square every index must be even, so multiply by 2 × 3: pk = 2⁴ × 3² × 5². So k = 6.
questions.tip: For a square number all the indices in the prime factorisation must be even; for a cube they must all be multiples of 3.

questions.q:
(a) Simplify (16x⁸)^(3/4). [2]
(b) Find the value of x when 9ˣ × 3 = 27^(x − 1). [2]
ms: (b) M1: writes all terms as powers of 3, e.g. 3^(2x + 1) = 3^(3x − 3)
questions.tip: Write every term with the same base before you compare indices.

questions.q:
Do not use a calculator in this question.
(a) Show that (√12 + √3)² = 27. [2]
(b) Write (6 + √2)/(3 − √2) in the form (a + b√2)/c, where a, b and c are integers. [3]
ms: (b) M1: multiplies numerator and denominator by (3 + √2)
(b) M1: denominator 9 − 2 = 7 seen, or numerator expanded to 4 correct terms 18 + 6√2 + 3√2 + 2
questions.tip: In a 'show that' question every step must be written; jumping straight to 27 scores only the final mark at best.

questions.q:
(a) Show that the recurring decimal 0.21̇5̇ (= 0.2151515…) can be written as 71/330. [3]
(b) Write down an irrational number between 4 and 5. [1]
(c) Show that √8 × √18 is a rational number. [2]
ms: (a) M1: subtracts two correct equations to remove the recurring part, e.g. 1000x − 10x = 213 so 990x = 213
(b) B1: any correct irrational, e.g. √17, √20, π + 1 (not a recurring or terminating decimal)
(c) A1: = 12, which is an integer so rational
questions.model:
(a) Let x = 0.2151515…
Then 10x = 2.151515… and 1000x = 215.151515…
1000x − 10x = 215.1515… − 2.1515… so 990x = 213
x = 213/990 = 71/330 (dividing top and bottom by 3).
(b) √20 (because 4 = √16 and 5 = √25).
(c) √8 × √18 = √144 = 12. 12 = 12/1 can be written as a fraction of integers, so it is rational.
questions.tip: Choose two multiples of x whose decimal parts are identical; here 10x and 1000x both end in .151515…
